title: Pacing strategies: how to spread the effort
goal: Name the six pacing profiles and explain which one wins in short, middle and long events, using world-record and race data.

steps.title: Six shapes of a race
steps.text:
Your [pacing strategy](g:pacing-strategy) is how you spread work and energy over a race, and it can make a large difference to the result [[c:pacing-matters]]. Plot speed or power against distance and six shapes turn up [[c:six-profiles]]:

| profile | shape |
|---|---|
| [all-out](g:all-out-pacing) | flat out from the gun, fading to the line |
| [positive](g:positive-pacing) | fastest early, then slowing |
| [negative](g:negative-pacing) | speeding up over the race |
| [even](g:even-pacing) | the same all the way |
| [parabolic](g:parabolic-pacing) | U, J or reverse J: fast start, slower middle, fast finish |
| [variable](g:variable-pacing) | ups and downs with the course, wind or rivals |

A burst of speed near the finish is an [end spurt](g:end-spurt).

claims.text: How an athlete spreads work and energy over an event can have a large effect on performance.

evidence.quote: It is widely recognized that an athlete's 'pacing strategy', or how an athlete distributes work and energy throughout an exercise task, can have a significant impact on performance.

claims.text: Six pacing profiles are described: negative, all-out, positive, even, parabolic and variable.

evidence.quote: These include the negative, all-out, positive, even, parabolic-shaped and variable pacing strategies.

steps.title: Short events: go from the gun
steps.text:
In very short events the start matters most. For efforts of about 30 s or less, an explosive [all-out](g:all-out-pacing) start seems best [[c:short-allout]].

Why? At the start you are slow: you must get the body (and the bike) up to speed from nothing, and in a short race those seconds are a big share of the total. The time saved by a hard start outweighs the speed lost to fatigue in the last metres.

Modelling of cycling time trials gives a rule of thumb: for 2 min or less, start maximally; up to about 10 min, start harder than the average power, but not flat out [[c:tt-start-rule]]. The longer the race, the more a fast start costs later.

claims.text: Events of about 30 s or less may benefit from an all-out start; in events over about 2 min, more even pacing may improve times.

evidence.quote: Research suggests that extremely short-duration events (< or =30 seconds) may benefit from an explosive 'all-out' strategy, whereas during prolonged events (>2 minutes), performance times may be improved if athletes distribute their pace more evenly.

claims.text: In cycling time trials of 2 min or less the start should be maximal; up to about 10 min the starting effort should be raised.

evidence.quote: For a shorter TT (< or = 10 minutes), work rate should be increased during the starting effort because this proportion of total race time is significant.

For a very short TT (< or = 2 minutes), the starting effort should be maximal, since the time saved during the starting phase is predicted to outweigh any time lost during the final metres because of fatigue.

steps.title: Longer events: even wins, but few start even
steps.text:
In a time trial longer than about 10 min in steady conditions (a velodrome, no wind), an [even](g:even-pacing) spread of power is best [[c:long-even]].

Yet riders start too hard. In a 16.1 km lab time trial (headwind for the first half, tailwind for the second), 7 cyclists chose 267 W for the first 1.6 km: 14% above their race average of 235 W. Then they fell below it [[c:start-too-fast]].

Ridden again at the same average power, held steady, the course took about 10 s less [[c:constant-faster]].

Why? Air resistance rises steeply with speed, so the extra watts of a hard start buy little speed, while riding far above [critical power](g:critical-power) early brings fatigue that costs more later.

claims.text: In time trials over about 10 min in stable conditions, an even distribution of power is optimal.

evidence.quote: When environmental conditions are relatively stable (e.g. in a velodrome) and the TT is >10 minutes, then an even distribution of work rate is optimal.

claims.text: In a self-paced 16.1 km time trial, riders' power over the first 1.61 km was 14% above their race average.

evidence.quote: In the ITT, riders chose a mean +/- SD power output of 267 +/- 56 W in the first 1.61 km which was 14% higher than the overall race mean +/- SD of 235 +/- 41 W.

claims.text: Riding the same average power at a constant level was about 10 s faster than the self-paced ride.

evidence.quote: riders habitually set off too fast in the first few kilometres and will benefit (10 s improvement) from a constant pacing strategy

steps.title: What world records look like
steps.text:
World records show pacing that worked at the top. Men's track records from 1912 to 2004 show [[c:wr-800]]:

- **800 m:** the first lap is faster than the second (on average about 52 s against 54 s); only 2 of 26 records had a faster second lap. A [positive](g:positive-pacing) profile.
- **5,000 and 10,000 m:** the first and last kilometres are faster than the middle ones: an even pace with an [end spurt](g:end-spurt) [[c:wr-endspurt]].

An end spurt means a reserve was kept through the middle: even in a record, the runner wasn't at the limit until the end.

In the 2008 and 2011 marathon world records, neither runner held an even pace once hills and wind were allowed for [[c:marathon-wr]].

claims.text: In men's 800 m world records the second lap was slower than the first, and faster in only 2 records.

evidence.quote: The second lap in the 800-m event was significantly slower than the first lap (52.0 + or - 1.7 vs 54.4 + or - 4.9 seconds, P < .00005).
In only 2 world records was the second lap faster than the first lap.

claims.text: In 5,000 and 10,000 m world records an end spurt occurs because a reserve is kept in the middle part of the race.

evidence.quote: In the 5000-m and 10,000-m events, an end spurt occurs because of the maintenance of a reserve during the middle part of the race.

claims.text: In two marathon world records, neither runner followed even pacing after adjusting for gradient and headwind.

evidence.quote: After adjusting for these responses, neither runner followed the (optimal) 'even' power pacing principle

steps.title: Races are not record attempts
steps.text:
Records are run against the clock, championships against rivals. In the 2008 Olympic finals from 800 to 10,000 m, the pacing of 133 finalists differed from world-record patterns in 6 of 8 races. In the long finals, pace changed every 100 m by 1.6–2.7% on average, and every race was decided in the last lap [[c:olympic-variable]]. Contenders used [variable](g:variable-pacing) pace to break the field.

For middle distances (1.5–2 min) and the longest events (over about 4 h), nobody yet knows the best pacing; well-trained athletes tend to pace positively, slowing gradually after an early peak [[c:ultra-positive]].

So 'even is best' is a rule for the clock. To win, you may have to pace against people.

claims.text: In the 2008 Olympic long-distance track finals pace varied every 100 m by 1.6–2.7%, and all races were decided in the final lap.

evidence.quote: In the long distance finals, runners varied their pace every 100 m by a mean 1.6-2.7%.
All races were decided during the final lap.

claims.text: In middle-distance and ultra-endurance events the optimal pacing is unknown; well-trained athletes tend to pace positively.

evidence.quote: However, evidence suggests that during these events well trained athletes tend to adopt a positive pacing strategy, whereby after peak speed is reached, the athlete progressively slows.

points: Six pacing profiles: all-out, positive, negative, even, parabolic (U, J or reverse J) and variable.
About 30 s or less: all-out. Cycling time trials up to about 2 min: maximal start; up to about 10 min: a start harder than average.
Longer, in steady conditions: even pacing is best, yet even trained riders start too hard.
World records: the 800 m is run positive; the 5,000 and 10,000 m even with an end spurt, a sign of a kept reserve.
Championship races are paced against rivals: variable, decided in the last lap. Records only show pacing that succeeded.

variants.stem: A runner covers the first half of a half marathon in 52 min and the second half in 49 min. Which pacing profile is this?

options.text: Negative
options.why: Right: the second half is faster, so speed rises over the race.

options.text: Positive
options.why: Positive pacing means slowing down: the first half would be the faster one.

options.text: Even
options.why: 3 min over about 50 min is about 6%: too big a change to call even.

options.text: All-out
options.why: All-out means flat out from the start and fading; it suits only very short events.

variants.stem: A cyclist averages 310 W over the first 10 km of a 40 km time trial, then 295, 285 and 270 W over the next three 10 km blocks. Which pacing profile is this?

options.text: Positive
options.why: Right: power is highest early and falls steadily.

options.text: Negative
options.why: Negative pacing would mean power rising over the race; here it falls.

options.text: Parabolic
options.why: A parabolic profile needs a fast finish; this one only declines.

options.text: Variable
options.why: Variable means ups and downs; this is a steady fall, not swings.

variants.stem: A 10,000 m runner's kilometre splits: 2:38 for the first, then eight between 2:42 and 2:44, then 2:33 for the last. Which profile is this?

options.text: Parabolic (U-shaped)
options.why: Right: fast start, even middle, fastest finish: the U shape seen in 10,000 m world records.

options.text: Positive (slowing)
options.why: Positive means slowing to the end, but the last kilometre is the fastest.

options.text: Negative (speeding up)
options.why: The first kilometre is faster than the middle ones, so speed doesn't rise throughout.

options.text: All-out (flat out)
options.why: All-out is flat out from the start for very short events; this is a 27 min race with a steady middle.

variants.stem: In a draft-legal triathlon, a triathlete's bike power swings between about 150 W through corners and 450 W out of them and on climbs, with no upward or downward trend over the 40 km. Which profile is this?

options.text: Variable
options.why: Right: repeated ups and downs set by the course and the pack, with no overall trend.

options.text: Even
options.why: Even pacing means steady power; swings from 150 to 450 W are the opposite.

options.text: Positive
options.why: Positive pacing needs a downward trend over the race; there is none here.

options.text: Parabolic
options.why: Parabolic means one fast start and one fast finish around a slower middle, not repeated swings.

variants.stem: Why does an all-out start suit a 30 s track sprint but not a 10 km run?

options.text: In a short race, time spent getting up to speed is a large share of the total, and little time is left for fatigue to cost you
options.why: Right: the time saved early outweighs the speed lost at the end in short events only.

options.text: Short sprints use no energy from oxygen, so fatigue can't build up during them
options.why: Fatigue builds very fast in sprints (phosphocreatine falls within seconds), and even 30 s has an aerobic share.

options.text: Muscles can't change speed once a short race has begun, so the first second fixes the pace
options.why: Speed changes all through a sprint; it rises and then fades.

options.text: Long races need a slow start because muscles only work well once they are warm
options.why: Warming up happens before the start; the reason to hold back is the cost of fatigue later.

variants.stem: A track cyclist rides a 1 km time trial lasting about 65 s. Based on the modelling evidence, how should she start?

options.text: Maximally, accepting that power fades at the end
options.why: Right: for time trials of 2 min or less the start should be maximal.

options.text: At even power from start to finish
options.why: Even power is the rule for time trials over about 10 min in steady conditions.

options.text: Easy for the first lap, then build up
options.why: A slow start wastes time while the bike is slow; nothing at the end can win it back in 65 s.

options.text: At average power, saving a sprint for the last 200 m
options.why: In a 65 s effort the time saved at the start is worth more than a late sprint.

variants.stem: A 4 km individual pursuit on the track lasts about 4.5 min. How should the start compare with the average power for the race?

options.text: Harder than average, but short of maximal
options.why: Right: up to about 10 min the starting effort should be raised; only at 2 min or less is it maximal.

options.text: Maximal, as in a 1 km time trial
options.why: The maximal start is for efforts of 2 min or less; over 4.5 min it would cost too much later.

options.text: Exactly at average power from the gun
options.why: Even pacing from the gun is the rule for efforts over about 10 min.

options.text: Easier than average, saving energy for the finish
options.why: That is a negative split; it loses time while the bike accelerates.

variants.stem: In a lab 16.1 km time trial, a rider rides the first 1.6 km 14% above his race average and then drops below it. Ridden again at the same average power but held constant, he is about 10 s faster. What does this show?

options.text: His chosen start was too hard: the time it bought was less than the later slowdown cost
options.why: Right: same average power, better spread, faster time.

options.text: The constant ride used more energy in total
options.why: Average power, and so total work, was the same in both rides.

options.text: A fast start always pays, because time banked early is never lost
options.why: Here the fast start was the slower ride overall.

options.text: Riding by feel gives better pacing than riding to a set power
options.why: He rode by feel in the first trial, and that was the slower one.

variants.stem: How were men's 800 m world records usually paced?

options.text: First lap faster than the second
options.why: Right: about 52 s against 54 s on average; only 2 of 26 had a faster second lap.

options.text: Second lap faster than the first
options.why: That happened in only 2 of 26 records.

options.text: Two laps run to within a tenth of a second
options.why: The laps differed by about 2 s on average.

options.text: A slow first lap, then a long end spurt
options.why: That describes no 800 m pattern; the end spurt belongs to the 5,000 and 10,000 m records.

variants.stem: How were men's 5,000 and 10,000 m world records usually paced?

options.text: Fast first kilometre, even middle, fastest last kilometre
options.why: Right: an even pace with an end spurt, a U shape.

options.text: Fastest early, then slowing steadily to the finish
options.why: That is the positive pattern of the 800 m, not of the longer records.

options.text: Each kilometre faster than the one before
options.why: The middle kilometres were even, not getting faster all the time.

options.text: All-out from the start, holding on to the finish
options.why: All-out pacing suits efforts of about 30 s or less, not 13 or 27 min races.

variants.stem: A 10,000 m world-record runner runs his last kilometre faster than any before it. What does this end spurt suggest about the middle of the race?

options.text: He kept a reserve: he could have run faster there but held back
options.why: Right: an end spurt is possible only if something was kept back.

options.text: He was at his absolute limit in the middle, and the spurt came from a second wind
options.why: At a true limit he couldn't speed up; a 'second wind' doesn't explain a faster last kilometre.

options.text: His muscle glycogen had run out, so he switched to fat for the finish
options.why: Running on fat would make him slower, not faster.

options.text: The spurt was only possible because the pacemakers did the work
options.why: Pacemakers drop out before the end; the spurt comes from the runner's own reserve.

variants.stem: A coach says: "World records show the optimal pacing, so copy their splits." What most limits that conclusion?

options.text: Records include only the runs that worked; failed attempts with the same pacing are never counted
options.why: Right: selecting only successes is a bias; observational records can't show that a pacing caused the result.

options.text: Records are too old to say anything about today's athletes
options.why: The analysis ran to 2004 and the patterns were consistent over decades; age isn't the main problem.

options.text: Lap times in records are measured too roughly to show any pattern
options.why: Lap and kilometre splits are timed well enough to show 2 s differences.

options.text: World records are set by too few countries to generalise
options.why: Nationality isn't the issue; the problem is that only successful runs are analysed.

variants.stem: Olympic 5,000 m finalists vary their pace far more than world-record runners do. Which explanation fits the evidence best?

options.text: They race to win, not for time: surges break the field and the race is decided in the last lap
options.why: Right: all 2008 finals were decided in the final lap, with top contenders using variable pace.

options.text: Olympic finalists are less fit than record holders, so they can't hold an even pace
options.why: Finalists include record holders; the difference comes from tactics, not fitness.

options.text: Championship tracks are slower, so the pace has to change
options.why: Track surfaces are similar; the swings follow rivals' moves.

options.text: Even pacing can't be sustained beyond 5 km
options.why: World records at 10,000 m show an even middle pace.
